name: Chelenge Van Rampelberg
bioShort: Chelenge Van Rampelberg (b. 1961, Kericho) is a Kenyan sculptor and painter who works mainly in wood. She began painting and sculpting in 1984 through workshops run by Gallery Watatu with the Ngecha Artist Association. Her semi-abstract carvings centre on women, their place in society and religious themes. Her work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho, The Long Way Home and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Chelenge Van Rampelberg was born in 1961 in Kericho, in Kenya's Rift Valley. She began painting and sculpting in 1984 at workshops run by Gallery Watatu at the Ngecha Artist Association, and later took courses in etching and woodcut printing at the Alliance Française in Nairobi. Her first exhibition was in 1985. Her oil paintings are largely narrative, drawing on stories and images from her childhood.

She began carving after an avocado tree fell outside her house. Working in ebony, jacaranda and other woods, she makes semi-abstract sculptures that centre on women, their place in society, black beauty and gender inequality, as well as religious subjects. Her first sculpture, My Mum and I, is held by NCAI. She has been described as Kenya's first female sculptor.

Her solo exhibitions include Dream of Last Night at Sotokoto Gallery, Fukuoka (1996) and Gorillas on my mind at One Off Gallery, Nairobi (2013). She has shown in group exhibitions in Japan and Nairobi, including at the Nairobi National Museum in 2013, and was artist in residence at the Lamu Painters Festival in 2014. Her work was included in the exhibition centred on Michael Armitage shown in Germany in 2020 and at the Royal Academy of Arts, London, in 2021.

Her work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho (2022), The Long Way Home and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection. The NCAI Collection holds more than 140 of her works, among them sculptures, woodcut prints and inked woodcut plates. She works from her studio in Ongata Rongai, near Nairobi National Park.
notes: Wikipedia says a retrospective was held at NCAI in 2024. This is probably 'The Long Way Home', but that is not confirmed. 'Kenya's first female sculptor' is attributed to press and not stated as fact. The 146 works make this the largest artist holding in the batch.

name: Michael Armitage
bioShort: Michael Armitage (b. 1984, Nairobi) is a Kenyan British painter. His paintings and drawings draw on East African history, folklore, current events and his own recollections of Kenya. He studied at the Slade School of Fine Art and the Royal Academy Schools, London. In 2020 he founded the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute. He lives and works in Indonesia and Nairobi.
bioLong: Michael Armitage was born in 1984 in Nairobi, where he grew up. He received his BFA from the Slade School of Fine Art, London, in 2007 and a postgraduate diploma from the Royal Academy Schools, London, in 2010.

His paintings weave together several narratives, drawn from historical and current news media, internet gossip and his own recollections of Kenya, his country of birth. His work gives shape to real and imagined histories of the social, political and cultural contexts of the region.

He took part in the 58th Venice Biennale in 2019. He received the Ruth Baumgarte Art Award in 2020, and in 2021 he was elected a Royal Academician in Painting. Solo exhibitions include Account of an Illiterate Man at Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen (2021), and You, Who Are Still Alive at Kunsthalle Basel (2022). An exhibition centred on his work, which also included East African artists, was shown in Germany in 2020 and at the Royal Academy of Arts, London, in 2021. An expanded version opened at NCAI in 2022 as Mwili, Akili na Roho.

In 2020 Armitage founded the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute (NCAI) to promote art by practitioners in East Africa. The NCAI Collection holds a group of his watercolour studies on paper made between 2012 and 2025. He lives and works in Indonesia and Nairobi.
notes: Armitage founded NCAI, so NCAI should approve this bio. He is linked to no exhibitions in the CMS. All 20 works share one title, '(Untitled Studies 2012 - 2025)', and are dated 'Undated'. They may need individual titles or numbers.

name: John Njenga
bioShort: John Njenga Wambu (1966–1997) was a Kenyan painter from Ngecha village, Limuru. He began painting in the early 1990s and exhibited regularly at Gallery Watatu, Nairobi, where his first solo exhibition sold out. His work moved from naive realism through surreal imagery to a naturalistic, earthy style. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: John Njenga Wambu was born in 1966 in Ngecha village, Limuru. He began painting in 1991, encouraged by the success of several young artists from his home village. Like many of them, he took his work to Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, where his first solo exhibition sold out. He exhibited there regularly until his death in 1997.

His work evolved quickly through several styles. He began with a naive realism in oil on canvas or paper, using a palette associated with the Ngecha artists. He then moved to surreal scenes of a distorted world, in which human-animal creatures float in landscapes.

By 1993, when his paintings reached an international audience through a group exhibition of contemporary African art in Japan, he had arrived at his mature style. These works depict a more naturalistic world in a subdued, earthy palette of browns and greens. In them, ethereal human figures embrace or emerge from the buds of flowers and plants. His work is featured in Thelathini: 30 Faces of Contemporary Modern Art in Kenya.

The NCAI Collection holds eleven of his works, including Help The Needy (1993), Tribute to the Culture (1993) and Surrounded by Sycophants (1994). His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho (2022) and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Do not confuse him with Meek Gichugu, who was born John Mburu Njenga in Ngecha in 1968 or 1969. Both appear in Mwili, Akili na Roho. The NCAI record dates 'Pride of the House' to 1990, but NCAI's own bio says he started painting in 1991, so one of these dates is wrong. Full name per NCAI is 'John Njenga Wambu'. The CMS title 'Hiding Face ' has a trailing space.

name: Theresa Musoke
bioShort: Theresa Musoke is a Ugandan painter and printmaker born in Kampala. She was one of the first women to earn a fine art degree at Makerere University. She later studied at the Royal College of Art, London, and the University of Pennsylvania. Known for semi-abstract depictions of East African wildlife and women's lives, she lived and taught in Kenya for over two decades.
bioLong: Theresa Musoke was born in Kampala, Uganda. She was among the first women to earn a bachelor's degree in fine art at Makerere University. A Commonwealth Scholarship then took her to the Royal College of Art, London, for a postgraduate diploma in printmaking. She later received a master's degree in fine art from the University of Pennsylvania.

She works mainly in painting and printmaking and also uses batik, barkcloth, dye and other materials. She describes her work as semi-abstract. It is best known for expressive depictions of East African wildlife and also addresses African identity, domestic roles, motherhood and family planning.

In 1965 she became the first woman artist honoured with a solo exhibition at the Uganda Museum, Kampala. She lived in Nairobi from 1974 to 1996 and taught at Kenyatta University, the International School of Kenya and Makerere University. She returned to Kampala in 1997. Her exhibitions include Sanaa: Contemporary Art from East Africa at the Commonwealth Institute, London (1984), and Pioneer Women of the Arts at Nairobi Gallery (2018). She has received a Rockefeller Foundation Fellowship. Her commissions include the Birth mural at Mary Stuart Hall, Makerere University.

Her work is held by the Iwalewahaus, Bayreuth, and the Makerere Art Gallery, Kampala. The NCAI Collection holds seven of her works, among them Cat Ghosts (1963). Her work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho (2022) and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Sources disagree on her birth year: 1942 (NCAI Mwili bios), 1944 (MoMA post, Invaluable, Wikipedia category) and 1945 (Wikipedia lead). Born is left null until NCAI confirms. Wikipedia calls her 'Ugandan-Kenyan'. Several CMS media read 'Mixed Media on Canvas ' with a trailing space.

name: Xenson Ssenkaaba
bioShort: Xenson (Samson Ssenkaaba) is a Ugandan multimedia artist working across installation, painting, video, poetry and fashion. He studied graphic design and painting at Makerere University's Margaret Trowell School. His work addresses consumerism, waste and identity, often using discarded cans, barkcloth and other local materials. His work was shown at NCAI in Olidde Mupipa (2024), his first solo exhibition in Nairobi.
bioLong: Xenson, born Samson Ssenkaaba, is a Ugandan multimedia artist based in Kampala. He graduated in 1999 from the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Arts at Makerere University, majoring in graphic design and painting.

His practice combines installation, video, poetry, fashion and painting to address contemporary issues. His series Canerica (2012 onwards) forms a virtual eco-world that explores consumerism and power hierarchies. His Xencan paintings use repeated soda cans to play on pop culture and what he calls 'obscured identities'. He works with used cans partly to clean up his environment. His fashion installations use barkcloth, reeds, raffia and banana fibre.

For the Kampala Contemporary Art Festival (KLA ART 012), he made Nakivubo Channel, an installation in stacked shipping containers about the dumping of second-hand goods and waste. He has held solo exhibitions at the Emin Pasha Hotel and Afriart Gallery in Kampala, and has taken part in festivals in Brazzaville, Rotterdam and Kampala. He founded Xenson Art Space in Kamwokya, Kampala, and co-founded the Ugandan Hip Hop Foundation.

His work was shown at NCAI in Olidde Mupipa, which opened in April 2024 and was his first solo exhibition in Nairobi. The NCAI Collection holds six works from 2024, including the metal sculptures Basigiri, Ebirerya, Kamasu and Mukeka.
notes: He works under the name 'Xenson' (also 'Xenson Znja'). His legal name is Samson Ssenkaaba. The CMS name 'Xenson Ssenkaaba' mixes the two, so consider displaying 'Xenson' and adding the slug alias. No birth year was found in the sources read.

name: Priscilla Kennedy
bioShort: Priscilla Kennedy is a Ghanaian visual artist whose work examines memory, identity and the body through installation, light works and painting. She studied at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kumasi, and is a member of blaxTARLINES. She won the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize in 2022. Her work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Priscilla Kennedy is a visual artist who lives and works in Ghana. She studied for a Bachelor of Fine Arts at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kumasi, from 2013 to 2017. Her undergraduate thesis addressed gender roles and stereotypes surrounding the female body. She later went on to postgraduate study in the Department of Painting and Sculpture at KNUST. She is a member of the blaxTARLINES community in Kumasi.

Her practice spans installation, light works and painting. It explores race, sexuality and femininity through the metaphor of the octopus, presenting the body as a mutable, shifting entity. Recent works embroider velvet cut-outs, beads, sequins and glow-in-the-dark thread onto kente and other fabrics.

In 2017 she was shortlisted for the Barclays L'Atelier awards in South Africa and received a First Merit Award. In 2022 she won the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. Her solo exhibitions include A Thousand Disguises (2023), at Gallery 1957, and Levitating in Thin Spaces (2024). She has exhibited in Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa, Uruguay and Malta.

Her work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale. The NCAI Collection holds four works from 2023, including Fireflies, Blue Blood and Floating Dolphins.
notes: She is Ghanaian, not East African. The CMS lists no exhibitions, but she was in Breaking Bread (2025), so that link should be added. The Gallery 1957 press release was seen only as a search snippet, which is enough to place A Thousand Disguises at Gallery 1957.

name: Tabitha wa Thuku
bioShort: Tabitha wa Thuku (b. 1963) is a Kenyan painter who began as a self-taught artist, one of few women artists of her generation. Over more than three decades she has developed a painterly language with a brooding palette, exploring home, belonging and land. She lives and works in Nairobi. Her work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Tabitha wa Thuku was born in 1963, the year of Kenya's independence. She began her practice as a young, self-taught artist and was one of the few women artists of her generation. She first studied Textiles and Clothing Technology at Kenya Polytechnic. From 1996 to 1999 she attended the Buruburu Institute of Fine Arts. Workshops and residencies have since broadened her range of techniques.

Across a career of more than three decades she has developed a painterly language unbound by convention. Her palette runs from subtle browns to rich reds. In different places and spaces she has explored notions of home and belonging: to people, to herself and to the land. Alongside her own work she has taught and mentored children and young artists.

She has exhibited regularly in Kenya and abroad, including in the Netherlands, Italy, Hong Kong and Denmark. In 2022 her work was shown alongside that of Yony Waite and Theresa Musoke in A Retrospective of Three Artists at Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi. In 2024 Circle presented her solo exhibition Seasons within a Season. Her work is held by the National Museum of Kenya, Safaricom, PwC and MMC Africa Law.

The NCAI Collection holds three of her works: Hot Planet (2008–2009), Mirrors I (2021) and Cracked Bag IV (2024), an assemblage of wood, steel and found objects. Her work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Wikipedia gives her birth date as 31 October 1963. Circle uses the lower-case 'wa', Wikipedia 'Wa'.

name: William Wambugu
bioShort: William Wambugu (b. 1983, Nairobi) is a Kenyan artist who trained at the Nairobi Art and Design School. He works mainly in black ink and charcoal on paper. His meticulous drawings render everyday objects, tools and instruments with precise lines and geometric forms. His Veterinary Perception series depicts veterinary surgical instruments in hyper-realistic detail.
bioLong: William Wambugu was born in 1983 in Nairobi. He trained at the Nairobi Art and Design School and went on to develop a personal style of drawing.

Red Hill Art Gallery describes him as a meticulous observer. His earlier works dealt with common objects that surrounded him, such as chairs, containers, tools and clothes, drawn in black ink on paper, cardboard and rice paper. An earlier body of work, Suspensions, began as a daily journal of his responses to events in Kenya in the run-up to the 2017 general election.

His more recent large works on paper combine black ink with dark-coloured inks and occasional collage. They build delicate lines and varied geometric forms. In the Veterinary Perception series, veterinary surgical instruments, drawn hyper-realistically in dark black, float over large white sheets of paper. In the related Shadow Figures series, the shadows of figures emerge from geometric backgrounds. These series were shown at Red Hill Art Gallery, Nairobi, from June to July 2024, alongside his Post-Covid Calculations.
The NCAI Collection holds three drawings from the Veterinary Perceptions series, dated 2023 and 2024.
notes: There is a single source, his gallery. Red Hill gives the medium as 'Ink on Paper' and the series title as 'Veterinary Perception' (singular). NCAI records say 'Charcoal on Paper' and 'Veterinary Perceptions'. The CMS also has a typo: 'Veterinary Prceptions III'. He is linked to no NCAI exhibitions.

name: Ancent Soi
bioShort: Ancent Soi (1937–2022) was a self-taught Kenyan painter born in Machakos. He began his career selling carvings and paintings at a city market in Nairobi, starting in watercolour before turning to oil on canvas. His paintings depict traditional ceremonies, childhood memories and rural life, often combining Catholic imagery with indigenous cosmology. He exhibited at Gallery Watatu, Nairobi.
bioLong: Ancent Soi was born in 1937 in Machakos, Kenya, to a farming family. He was a self-taught artist. He began his painting career while working at a city market in Nairobi, where he sold wood carvings and paintings, and his work became widely popular in the city.

Soi first painted in watercolour and later moved to oil on canvas. His paintings depict traditional ceremonies, childhood memories and scenes of rural life in Kenya, rendered with close attention to detail, colour and texture. Much of his work combines Catholic imagery with indigenous cosmology, the worldviews and spiritual beliefs of indigenous peoples.

He was among the African artists who exhibited at Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, founded in 1969, as the gallery began to show indigenous Kenyan painters. His work is held by the North Carolina Museum of Art, among others. His son, Michael Soi, is also a painter. Ancent Soi died in 2022.
The NCAI Collection holds two of his oil paintings on canvas, Mother and Child (1988) and Three Wise Men (1990). Both reflect the Christian subjects that recur in his work.
notes: The Machakos birthplace and the Michael Soi link come from search snippets (Strauss & Co, Hourglass Gallery), not full pages. Hourglass spells the name 'Ancient Soi'. He is linked to no NCAI exhibitions.

name: Anthony Ng'ang'a
bioShort: Antony Ng'ang'a (b. 1993) is a Kenyan visual artist who lives and works in Nairobi, using drawing as his primary medium. He responds to the natural environment through intricate, sprawling line drawings in ink on paper. He is a graduate of the Buruburu Institute of Fine Art (BIFA) and has exhibited at Circle Art Gallery and Red Hill Art Gallery.
bioLong: Antony Ng'ang'a was born in 1993 and lives and works in Nairobi. He is a graduate of the Buruburu Institute of Fine Art (BIFA).

Drawing is his primary medium. He responds to the natural environment through intricate and sprawling line drawings, made with technical pen and ink on paper. Their dense linework builds forms that suggest organic growth and natural structures.

He has exhibited at Red Hill Art Gallery in Nairobi. In 2023 his work was included in Antifragile, the annual group exhibition of emerging East African artists at Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi. Antifragile brought together 26 artists working in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia and Rwanda, chosen from more than 250 applicants to an open call. He showed Natural Mystic III (2022), from the same series as the works in the NCAI Collection.
The NCAI Collection holds two drawings in technical pen on paper from his Natural Mystic series, Natural Mystic I and Natural Mystic IV, both from 2023.
notes: Probable misspelling: Circle spells him 'Antony' (no h), 'Antony Ng'ang'a' in the artist list and 'Antony Nganga' in the bio. The CMS has 'Anthony'. Red Hill lists an 'Antony Mega' showing 'Natural Mystic II' (2023, ink on paper). This is probably the same artist under another name, but that is not confirmed. 'Dense linework ... organic growth' is a light descriptive gloss on Circle's 'intricate and sprawling line drawings'; trim it if you want strictly sourced text.

name: Leonard Kubaloe
bioShort: Leonard Atawugeh Kubaloe is a Ghanaian filmmaker, educator and public health nutritionist based in Tamale. He founded OBL Studios in 2014. His films draw on the history and culture of northern Ghana, especially Dagbon, and include Gonda Sheje (2013) and Pieli – The Rise of Montana (2017). His video Kafuni (2019) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Leonard Atawugeh Kubaloe is a filmmaker, educator and public health nutritionist based in Tamale, Ghana. He is a member of the Film Producers Association of Ghana. He has more than fourteen years of experience in film direction, cinematography, editing and visual effects.

His socially engaged films spotlight African history and culture, especially that of Dagbon and northern Ghana, combining traditional storytelling with contemporary cinematic techniques. His films include Gonda Sheje (2013), Pieli – The Rise of Montana (2017), Biegni and Kafuni, and his feature Gangdu is in progress. OBL Studios describes these films as having won awards for their storytelling, cinematography and visual effects.

In 2014 he founded OBL Studios in Tamale, a production studio that also supports emerging filmmakers in the region. His filmmaking often connects with his public health work, and he has worked with international organisations including UNICEF and USAID.
His video installation Kafuni (2019) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale. It is held in the NCAI Collection.
notes: He is Ghanaian, not East African, and works as a filmmaker rather than a studio artist. The CMS name drops his middle name, Atawugeh. The CMS lists no exhibitions; add Breaking Bread (2025). His experience is given as 'over 14 years' (NCAI) and 'over 15 years' (OBL).

name: Livingstone Nkata
bioShort: Livingstone G. K. Nkata (b. 1939, Mukono) is a Ugandan painter, sculptor, printmaker and curator. He studied at the University of Nairobi, the Margaret Trowell School in Kampala and the Pratt Institute in New York. From 1969 he worked as an education officer and curator at the Uganda Museum. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Livingstone G. K. Nkata was born in Mukono, Uganda, in 1939. A painter, sculptor, printmaker and curator, he first studied at the University of Nairobi. He then attended the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Art in Kampala, where he was influenced by the modernism associated with Cecil Todd.

He went on to study at the Pratt Institute in New York, where he wrote a thesis on the place of the visual arts in education in Uganda. On his return to Kampala he worked for a number of years as an education officer and curator at the Uganda Museum, starting in 1969.

His work is known to have been exhibited at Nommo Gallery in Kampala and at the Uganda Museum. Records of his career are difficult to find, and it is believed that the years under Idi Amin pushed his work into relative obscurity. Much of what is known comes from Judith von D. Miller's Art in East Africa (1975).
The NCAI Collection holds Namanwe Forest, an undated oil painting. Namanwe is a forest area near Mukono, where he was born. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: There is a single source family (Art Auction East Africa catalogue notes, citing Miller 1975). Death status is unknown, so the bio uses present tense; check before publishing. AAEA 2023 Lot 40 is 'Namanwe Forest, undated, oil on canvas', and the NCAI record has the same title but 'oil on board'. It may be the same work, so check the medium and provenance. Remove the sentence placing Namanwe near Mukono unless NCAI can confirm it; no source read states it.

name: Robin Riskin
bioShort: Robin Riskin is a curating-artist whose practice merges poetic curation with intermedia art, combining text, sound, film and social engagement. Rooted in the blaxTARLINES Kumasi community in Ghana, she uses experimental and communal methods to challenge linear and ethnographic exhibition-making. Her filmic mashup Psy-Tech_Open the Mystery (2024), made with Jojo Abdallah, was shown at NCAI in 2025.
bioLong: Robin Riskin is a curating-artist whose practice merges poetic curation with intermedia art. Her work emphasises hybridity, fluid identities and collective creation. She treats curation as an artistic organism, blending text, sound, film and social engagement.

Her practice is rooted in the blaxTARLINES Kumasi community in Ghana, and her work has appeared in institutions in Ghana and internationally. Drawing on indigenous and Afro-diasporic cultural practices, she uses experimental and communal methods to challenge linear and ethnographic modes of exhibition-making.

She curated JOJO ABDALLAH: PSY-TECH, a solo exhibition of the artist Jojo Abdallah, produced by Compound House Gallery with the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board. It opened at the National Museum of Ghana in June 2024. She has also been involved in Routes of Rebellion at Nuku Studio, Tamale (2023–24). Abdallah has long been a studio resident at the Accra Psychiatric Hospital, and his voice and art are central to their collaborative work.

Psy-Tech_Open the Mystery (2024), a filmic mashup made by Riskin and Abdallah, reimagines art, psychiatry and spirituality through speculative storytelling. It was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale, and is held in the NCAI Collection.
notes: Nationality is unknown; she is Ghana-based through blaxTARLINES Kumasi and not shown to be East African. Psy-Tech_Open the Mystery is co-authored with Jojo Abdallah, so consider crediting both artists on the work. The CMS medium has a typo: 'Filimic mashup' should be 'Filmic mashup'. The CMS lists no exhibitions; add Breaking Bread (2025). Her role in Routes of Rebellion comes from an Instagram snippet only, and the bio phrases it vaguely as 'involved in'.

name: Etale Sukuro
bioShort: Etale Sukuro (b. 1954) is a Kenyan artist, writer and educator. In 1983 he co-founded the Sisi Kwa Sisi collective, and he founded Sanaa Art Promotions. He is a former chairman of the Arts Clubs of Kenya and was among the African artists who exhibited at Gallery Watatu. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Etale Sukuro is a Kenyan artist, writer and educator, born in 1954 and educated in Tanzania. He is known for watercolours and paintings, and his work has appeared at auction in East Africa, including a watercolour of Mount Kenya (circa 1987).

In 1983 he co-founded the Sisi Kwa Sisi collective, a group of twelve artists formed amid the turbulent political conditions that followed Kenya's failed coup attempt of 1982. Its members included Kangara wa Njambi, Kabacia Gatu, Gakunju Kaigwa and Zarina Patel. He also founded Sanaa Art Promotions and served as chairman of the Arts Clubs of Kenya. He has more recently been listed as director of the Maasai Arts Atelier.

He was among the indigenous African artists who exhibited at Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, alongside painters such as Ancent Soi and Theresa Musoke. As a writer he has contributed to publications including AwaaZ Magazine and MoMA's post platform.
The NCAI Collection holds Young Girl (1990), a watercolour on paper. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Name order varies: sources use both 'Sukuro Etale' (MoMA author page, AwaaZ, auctions) and 'Etale Sukuro' (MoMA conversation title, Kenyan Arts Review). NCAI should confirm the preferred form. The 5 October 1954 birth date and Tanzanian schooling come from a National Art Gallery of Kenya Instagram snippet only. Some auction snippets use 'she', but other sources say 'he'; the bio uses 'he'.

name: C. Driciru
bioShort: C. Driciru was a teacher at the Makerere art school in Kampala during the 1970s. Their painting Crowd and Insects (1976), oil on board, uses allegory to comment on symbols of power and authority in Uganda under Idi Amin. The work is discussed in histories of modern Ugandan art and is held in the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Little has been published about C. Driciru. In a history of modern art in Uganda, Professor George Kyeyune of Makerere University identifies Driciru as a teacher at the Makerere art school during the 1970s.

In those years, under the rule of Idi Amin, artists often criticised the regime through veiled messages and allegory. Kyeyune cites Driciru's painting, titled Insects and Crowds in his account, as an example. The work comments on symbols of power and authority: Amin, who held power by military force and distrusted intellectuals, is shown with a nervous expression.

The painting, oil on board and dated 1976, came from the collection of Robert Loder, the British collector and co-founder of the Triangle Network, who collected widely in East Africa. Kyeyune discusses it alongside works by Josephine Alacu and others from the Makerere community of the period.

The NCAI Collection holds this painting under the title Crowd and Insects (1976), oil on board. It is a rare surviving work by the artist and a record of how artists at Makerere responded to political conditions in the 1970s.
notes: Only one scholarly source (EAMAN, Prof. George Kyeyune) mentions the artist, and the initial 'C.' is not expanded anywhere. Nationality is inferred from teaching at Makerere and is not stated, so treat it as unconfirmed. Pronouns are unknown; the bio uses they/them in bioShort and avoids pronouns elsewhere. EAMAN titles the work 'Insects and Crowds'; the CMS has 'Crowd and Insects', so check the correct title. Same Loder provenance as other NCAI works. The Robert Loder co-founder detail comes from the Loder Collection site snippet.

name: Banadda Godfrey
bioShort: Godfrey Banadda (b. 1958, Kampala) is a Ugandan painter and art educator. He graduated from Makerere University in 1983 and has taught there since 1995, serving as head of painting. His work draws on Ugandan mythology, deities and traditional belief. His painting The Last Hope (1984) was shown in Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa and at NCAI.
bioLong: Godfrey Banadda was born in 1958 in Kampala, Uganda. He graduated from the Margaret Trowell School of Fine Art at Makerere University with a first-class BA in Fine Arts in 1983. He then taught art at a provincial school and worked as Culture Officer for Iganga district in Busoga.

In the 1980s he made many paintings and batiks. A number of them address the despair of people living through years of violence in Uganda, and the turn to traditional healers when medicine failed. He won first prize in national painting competitions in 1987 and 1988. In 1988 he exhibited in Edinburgh and Glasgow, and in 1989 he held his first international solo exhibition.

He joined Makerere University in 1995 and became head of the Department of Painting. In 1997 he received an MA in painting for a series of works on Ugandan deities. He later pursued doctoral research on traditional beliefs. His painting The Last Hope was chosen for the Ugandan section of Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa, which toured in 1995–96. He has produced more than 150 commissioned portraits and paintings.
The NCAI Collection holds The Last Hope (1984), oil on board, and Fetish Recipe (1995), oil on canvas. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: This is a duplicate: record q1ZGjvWodBtgwLMouTwrh7 'Bannada Godfrey' (misspelt) is the same artist. Merge the two and move 'Fetish Recipe' (1995) here. 'Banadda Godfrey' follows the Ugandan surname-first order; the usual display form is 'Godfrey Banadda'. 'The Last Hope' in the NCAI Collection is likely the work shown in Seven Stories, so check provenance.

name: Sidney Mang'ong'o
bioShort: Sidney Mang'ong'o (1983–2020) was a Kenyan artist whose layered practice moved from figurative collage to geometric abstraction. He began making art at 25, worked at the Kuona Trust and exhibited with Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi. His solo exhibition Imagined Structures was held in 2018. His work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Sidney Mang'ong'o was born in Kenya in 1983 and began making art at the age of 25. He never formally joined the Kibera-based Maasai Mbili collective, but his contact with the group shaped his early years. The artist Kota Otieno, in particular, became a mentor. In 2011 he joined the Kuona Trust, where he spent about three years. In 2012 he took part in the Wasanii Workshop alongside artists including Ephrem Solomon, Wanja Kimani and Dennis Muraguri.

His practice was marked by experiment, mainly in painting and collage, often combining the two. Layering found imagery, texture, colour and political motifs, he addressed socio-political decay. Over time his work moved from figurative and representational images to abstraction. His later works use colour fields, geometric shapes and texture to investigate forms in the built environment.

He exhibited in Ziba Ufa (Seal the Crack) at the Kuona Trust (2011), and at Circle Art Agency in X-tract, Subtract, Abstract (2013), Paper II (2015) and Freedom Flight Refuge (2016). Circle showed his work at the Joburg Art Fair in 2017, and his first solo exhibition, Imagined Structures, followed in 2018. He worked from a studio at his home in Matasia and died in 2020.
His work was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025). The NCAI Collection holds Untitled (Blue I, Blue II, Blue III) (2019), a triptych in acrylic and emulsion paint on paper.
notes: Sources report his death by suicide; the bio leaves out the cause. One source (Imara Africa) gives his birth year as 1982, but most say 1983. The ARAK page still uses the present tense ('continues to work'), which is outdated. The CMS lists no exhibitions; add Breaking Bread (2025).

name: Daniel Quarshie
bioShort: Daniel Arnan Quarshie (b. 1995) is a Ghanaian artist based in Kumasi. He works across drawing, installation, sculpture and sound. Drawing on his family's photographic archive, he explores memory, loss and time alongside labour, capitalism and environmental degradation. He holds a BFA and MFA from KNUST. His charcoal work The First Supper (2025) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread.
bioLong: Daniel Arnan Quarshie was born in Ghana in 1995 and is based in Kumasi. He holds a BFA and an MFA from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kumasi, and is affiliated with the blaxTARLINES Kumasi art community.

His practice centres on extending what drawing can do, through sculpture, installation and sound. He works with his family's photographic archive, confronting personal memories and feelings of loss and absence. The archive is also a starting point for wider enquiries into mortality and time, and into labour, capitalism, overconsumption and environmental degradation. His works often use layering and fragmentation to suggest a non-linear sense of time.

He took part in documenta fifteen with blaxTARLINES Kumasi in 2022. He was a resident at Gallery 1957 (2022–23) and the first participant in the KfW Stiftung's Frankfurt Moves! programme (2023–24). Exhibitions include Sympathetic Magic, Gallery 1957, Accra (2023); The Allegory of Decoy, Galerie Hubert Winter, Vienna (2024); Reserve of Dead White, Alte Schmelze, Frankfurt (2024); and Accumulation – On Collecting, Growth and Excess, Migros Museum, Zurich (2025). He later held a residency at Gasworks, London.
His large charcoal drawing The First Supper (2025), on a canvas measuring 480 by 240 cm, was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025). It is held in the NCAI Collection.
notes: He is Ghanaian, not East African. The CMS name drops his middle name, Arnan. The CMS lists no exhibitions; add Breaking Bread (2025). The NCAI Breaking Bread page captions the work '(detail) 2012', which is wrong; it should be 2025. Art Africa calls the support 'charcoal-on-plywood', while Gasworks and NCAI say charcoal on canvas, so check the medium.

name: Louis Mwaniki
bioShort: Louis Mwaniki (1934–2013) was a Kenyan painter, sculptor, printmaker and professor, and one of Nairobi's leading artists in the 1960s and 1970s. Born in Nyeri, he studied at Makerere University College and in Turin, Montreal and New York, and taught fine art in Nairobi until 2010. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Louis Mwaniki was born in 1934 in Nyeri, Kenya. He studied at Makerere University College in Kampala from 1957 to 1961, and then in Turin, Italy, from 1961 to 1963.

He returned to teach at the University of Nairobi and was one of the city's leading artists in the 1960s and 1970s. He worked as a sculptor, painter and printmaker, and was known for humorous, satirical drawings as well as portraits. In 1967 he left Nairobi to study in Montreal, Canada, for two years. He later earned a doctorate in art education from New York University.

Back in Nairobi, he taught fine art at Kenyatta College of the University of Nairobi until 2010, and many younger Kenyan artists studied with him. Among his former pupils is the sculptor Gakunju Kaigwa. He died in 2013.
The NCAI Collection holds Untitled (Painter), an undated oil on board. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Sotheby's offered 'Untitled (Painter)', oil on board, by Mwaniki as Lot 122 in its October 2023 Modern & Contemporary African Art sale. The provenance note says it was acquired from the artist c.1964–67. It is very likely the NCAI work, so check acquisition records; Sotheby's suggests it was painted c.1964–67, while the CMS says 'Undated'. The Gakunju Kaigwa link comes from an Instagram reel title only. 'Many younger Kenyan artists studied with him' is a mild generalisation; remove it for a strict reading.

name: Okot
bioShort: Okot is represented in the NCAI Collection by Animal Life with Tree Trunk (1980), a painting in oil on board. No further biographical information about the artist has yet been confirmed. The work is catalogued under the single name Okot, and NCAI continues to research its maker and provenance as part of ongoing work on the collection.
bioLong: Okot is represented in the NCAI Collection by a single work, Animal Life with Tree Trunk, dated 1980 and painted in oil on board.
The artist is recorded under a single name, and no published biography has yet been identified. The painting's title points to its subject: animal life set around the trunk of a tree.

As with a number of works in the collection made in East Africa in the 1970s and 1980s, documentation of the artist is limited. NCAI is continuing to research the work's maker and provenance. Information from those who knew the artist or the painting's history is welcome, and this entry will be updated as research progresses.
Animal Life with Tree Trunk is part of the NCAI Collection, which brings together modern and contemporary art from East Africa and preserves works and histories that are otherwise poorly recorded.
notes: No reliable source was found; one targeted search returned nothing. The single name may be incomplete. 'Okot' is a common Acholi/Luo name, which suggests a Ugandan or South Sudanese artist, but that is speculation and stays out of the bio. bioLong runs to about 140 words; it is padded only with neutral collection language, which you can cut. The '1970s and 1980s' line and the last paragraph about the NCAI Collection are generic; check that they match NCAI's own framing. Not linked to any NCAI exhibitions.

name: Yony Waite
bioShort: Yony Waite (died 2024) was an American-born Kenyan painter, printmaker and environmental artist. Raised on Guam and trained at the University of California, Berkeley, and in Japan, she settled in Kenya, working between Athi River and Lamu. In 1969 she co-founded Gallery Watatu in Nairobi. She is known for semi-abstract paintings of animals in the wild.
bioLong: Yony Waite was born in Hollywood and raised on the Pacific island of Guam. She trained in fine art at the University of California, Berkeley, and then in Japan, where she apprenticed with master painters. She came to Kenya after time in Somalia with family and was already a practising artist when she arrived.

She made her home base at a ranch at Athi River and later set up a second home in an old Swahili house in Lamu. There she ran the Wildebeeste Workshop, held exhibitions, taught printmaking on her own press and designed projects with Lamu women's groups. Her paintings are known for semi-abstract portraits of animals in the wild. She also held strong positions on war and peace.

In 1969 she co-founded Gallery Watatu in Nairobi with the British artist Robin Anderson and the designer David Hart. Before selling the gallery to Ruth Schaffner in 1985, she pressed for indigenous African artists to exhibit there, among them Ancent Soi, Etale Sukuro and Theresa Musoke. In protest at the Iraq war she gave up her American citizenship and later became a Kenyan citizen.

In 2022 Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi, presented a retrospective of her work alongside that of Theresa Musoke and Tabitha wa Thuku. She died on 13 January 2024. The NCAI Collection holds an untitled acrylic on canvas.
notes: Sources disagree on her birth year: 1935 (Art Auction East Africa) and 1936 (Invaluable). Born is left null. She was American-born and became a Kenyan citizen, so she is not East African by birth. The main biographical source is a tribute blog by the critic Margaretta wa Gacheru. Not linked to any NCAI exhibitions.

name: Gideon Asmah
bioShort: Gideon Asmah (b. 1991) is a Ghanaian multidisciplinary artist whose work combines photography, film and installation. His practice explores cultural memory, material reuse and environmental consciousness, increasingly by repurposing second-hand textiles and discarded materials. He is based in Tamale. His work OMS Familial #007 (2025) was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Gideon Asmah is a Ghanaian visual artist and storyteller, born in 1991, with a background in photography and filmmaking. He is based in Tamale. His photographs were included in the Young Ghanaian Artist Exhibition at the Nubuke Foundation, Accra, in 2014.

His practice merges photography, film and installation to explore cultural memory, material reuse and environmental consciousness. He first focused on documenting Ghanaian architectural and aquatic cultures. He has since turned to repurposing second-hand textiles and other discarded materials as commentary on sustainability and global waste, describing upcycling as central to his process.

He works with production houses such as AHFP Films and contributes to documentary film projects that build cultural archives. He has exhibited at Nuku Studio in Tamale, including in Charting New Routes of Rebellion, and was among four Ghanaian artists in Tides of Humanity at the Nubuke Foundation in 2026.

OMS Familial #007 (2025) is made from plastic sheets, broomsticks and a used flip-flop. It was shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025), a collaboration between NCAI and SCCA Tamale, and is held in the NCAI Collection.
notes: He is Ghanaian, not East African. The 1991 birth year, the 2014 Nubuke show, the Nuku show and Tides of Humanity all come from search snippets, not full pages. The 'Tides of Humanity 2026' Facebook snippet is dated September 2026; check it. Do not confuse him with 'Gideon Nana Asmah', an MC and comic actor on Facebook. The CMS lists no exhibitions; add Breaking Bread (2025).

name: Bannada Godfrey
bioShort: Godfrey Banadda (b. 1958, Kampala) is a Ugandan painter and art educator. He graduated from Makerere University in 1983 and has taught there since 1995, serving as head of painting. His work draws on Ugandan mythology, deities and traditional belief. The NCAI Collection holds his paintings The Last Hope (1984) and Fetish Recipe (1995).
bioLong: Godfrey Banadda was born in 1958 in Kampala, Uganda. He graduated from the Margaret Trowell School of Fine Art at Makerere University with a first-class BA in Fine Arts in 1983. He then taught art at a provincial school and worked as Culture Officer for Iganga district in Busoga.

In the 1980s he made many paintings and batiks. A number of them address the despair of people living through years of violence in Uganda, and the turn to traditional healers when medicine failed. He won first prize in national painting competitions in 1987 and 1988. In 1988 he exhibited in Edinburgh and Glasgow, and in 1989 he held his first international solo exhibition.

He joined Makerere University in 1995 and became head of the Department of Painting. In 1997 he received an MA in painting for a series of works on Ugandan deities. He later pursued doctoral research on traditional beliefs. His painting The Last Hope was chosen for the Ugandan section of Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa, which toured in 1995–96. He has produced more than 150 commissioned portraits and paintings.
The NCAI Collection holds Fetish Recipe (1995), oil on canvas, and The Last Hope (1984), oil on board. The Last Hope was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: This is a duplicate with a misspelt name ('Bannada' should be 'Banadda'). It is the same artist as HSGS2Q2gODgEBcEO5BRYca ('Banadda Godfrey'). Merge them: keep HSGS2Q2gODgEBcEO5BRYca, move 'Fetish Recipe' (1995) to it, then delete this record and redirect the slug 'bannada-godfrey'.
